messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints exactly one summary line per analysis in the form `E1 <title>: <finding with the key number>`. Use HC2 robust SEs. That is the only file you may write: never create helper or debug scripts; to inspect something, print it from 04_exploratory.py.
Run it with run_script. As soon as a run exits 0 with tables written, call in your NEXT turn
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":"one sentence for readers: what was compared and how, with no code, function or column names","table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Do not polish a script that already works. If one analysis keeps failing, delete it from the script and record the others.
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `reg.reestimate(hid, d)` re-fits registered hypothesis `hid` (e.g. "H1") with exactly its registered specification (exclusions, treatment arms, Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset `d` of the clean data and returns a DataFrame with one row per treatment arm (columns term, arm, estimate, std_error, p_value, conf_low, conf_high, n). `reg.reestimate(hid, d, moderator="col")` returns the arm x moderator interactions instead: one centred slope per arm for a numeric moderator, one row per level for a text or 0/1 column (bin a numeric moderator into a 0/1 column to compare two groups). These cover robustness checks and heterogeneity; do not build formulas or look up coefficient names yourself. `reg.HYPOTHESES` lists the hypothesis dicts (ids, outcomes, estimators). For anything else (e.g. a component item as the outcome), copy the hypothesis and change its outcome: `h = dict(reg.HYPOTHESES[0], outcome="item_col"); reg.reestimate(h, d)`. Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` first.
A robustness table must hold the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side (both from reg.reestimate). If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, drop that analysis.
Write rationales and methods in the third person (never 'I'). Call the plan's analyses 'planned', not 'registered', unless the study was pre-registered (see Registration in the task). Describe every variable only as the codebook does; a column the codebook does not describe is named by its column name (never call a knowledge score an attention check, for example). With several arms, a finding states the pattern across arms and how many estimates were tested, not just the most extreme one.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed; the turn after the first clean run, record_result with final=true. The last turn is reserved for record_result.

(outcome plausibility)

(outcome plausibility)
- X1: A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type. (outcome share)
- X2: A1. The slope of plausibility on trust in the sharer, by information type. (outcome plausibility)
- X3: A1. The close-tie premium on sharing, net of the other source attributes, by information type. (outcome share)
- X4: A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age. (outcome share_not_believe)
- X5: A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. (outcome share)
- X6: A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. Among misinformation profiles, sharing on the network's mean perceived belief in disputed claims, net of network ideological spread, mean trust, age and ideology. Each misinformation profile is weighted by 1 / the respondent's number of them, which reproduces the respondent-level regression of the misinformation-sharing rate. (outcome share)
- X7: B1. Message x respondent congruence: among partisan respondents shown partisan-slanted headlines, sharing of congenial against uncongenial content (headline slant from the paper's preliminary automated coding), by information type. (outcome share)
- X8: B2. A conspiracy-prone source: the slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims (0-1), net of the other source attributes, by information type. (outcome share)
- X9: B2. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims, by information type. (outcome plausibility)
- X10: B2, claim-specific (thin): for the anti-vaccine (polio) misinformation headline, plausibility when the sharer is seen as believing 'Covid-19 vaccines modify your DNA' against not. (outcome plausibility)
- X11: B3. Health vs. political misinformation: among misinformation profiles, the trust slope on sharing for health (guanabana, polio) and political headlines. (outcome share)
- X12: B3. Among misinformation profiles, the close-tie premium for health and political headlines. (outcome share)
- X13: B4. Sharer origin (continental US vs. elsewhere) and sharing, by survey language and by the respondent's nativity. (outcome share)

import importlib.util, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)

d = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
pathlib.Path('results').mkdir(exist_ok=True); pathlib.Path('figures').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def fmt(r):
    return "; ".join(f"{a} {e:.3f} (SE {s:.3f})" for a, e, s in zip(r.arm, r.estimate, r.std_error))

# E1 placebo-ish: effect on plausibility versus sharing (component outcome) -- plausibility outcome
h1 = reg.HYPOTHESES[0]
base = reg.reestimate(h1, d)
hp = dict(h1, outcome="plausibility")
pl = reg.reestimate(hp, d)
t1 = pd.concat([base.assign(outcome="share"), pl.assign(outcome="plausibility")])
t1.to_csv('results/E1_infotype_share_vs_plausibility.csv', index=False)
print("E1 Information type on sharing vs plausibility: " + fmt(base) + " | plausibility: " + fmt(pl))

# E2 robustness: drop respondents with age<25? use English-only and Spanish-only
rows = []
for lab, sub in [("All", d), ("English", d[d.survey_language == "English"]), ("Spanish", d[d.survey_language == "Spanish"])]:
    r = reg.reestimate(h1, sub); r["subset"] = lab; rows.append(r)
t2 = pd.concat(rows)
t2.to_csv('results/E2_infotype_by_language.csv', index=False)
print("E2 Information type effect on sharing by survey language: " + " | ".join(f"{l}: {fmt(g)}" for l, g in t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)))

# E3 heterogeneity by age (older vs younger than median)
d["older"] = (d.age > d.age.median()).astype(int)
t3 = reg.reestimate(h1, d, moderator="older")
t3.to_csv('results/E3_infotype_by_age.csv', index=False)
print("E3 Information type effect on sharing by age group: " + "; ".join(f"{r.arm}/{r.get('level', r.get('term'))} {r.estimate:.3f} (SE {r.std_error:.3f})" for r in t3.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for i, (lab, g) in enumerate(t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)):
    for j, r in enumerate(g.itertuples()):
        ax.errorbar(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2, xerr=1.96 * r.std_error, fmt='o', color='#b22' if lab == "All" else '#222')
        ax.text(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2 + 0.08, lab, fontsize=7, ha='center')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(g))); ax.set_yticklabels(list(g.arm))
ax.axvline(0, color='#222', lw=0.5)
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("Effect on sharing vs True/neutral")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/E2_language.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white')

{"path": "scripts/04_exploratory.py", "content": "import importlib.util, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)

d = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
pathlib.Path('results').mkdir(exist_ok=True); pathlib.Path('figures').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def fmt(r):
    return "; ".join(f"{a} {e:.3f} (SE {s:.3f})" for a, e, s in zip(r.arm, r.estimate, r.std_error))

# E1 placebo-ish: effect on plausibility versus sharing (component outcome) -- plausibility outcome
h1 = reg.HYPOTHESES[0]
base = reg.reestimate(h1, d)
hp = dict(h1, outcome="plausibility")
pl = reg.reestimate(hp, d)
t1 = pd.concat([base.assign(outcome="share"), pl.assign(outcome="plausibility")])
t1.to_csv('results/E1_infotype_share_vs_plausibility.csv', index=False)
print("E1 Information type on sharing vs plausibility: " + fmt(base) + " | plausibility: " + fmt(pl))

# E2 robustness: drop respondents with age<25? use English-only and Spanish-only
rows = []
for lab, sub in [("All", d), ("English", d[d.survey_language == "English"]), ("Spanish", d[d.survey_language == "Spanish"])]:
    r = reg.reestimate(h1, sub); r["subset"] = lab; rows.append(r)
t2 = pd.concat(rows)
t2.to_csv('results/E2_infotype_by_language.csv', index=False)
print("E2 Information type effect on sharing by survey language: " + " | ".join(f"{l}: {fmt(g)}" for l, g in t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)))

# E3 heterogeneity by age (older vs younger than median)
d["older"] = (d.age > d.age.median()).astype(int)
t3 = reg.reestimate(h1, d, moderator="older")
t3.to_csv('results/E3_infotype_by_age.csv', index=False)
print("E3 Information type effect on sharing by age group: " + "; ".join(f"{r.arm}/{r.get('level', r.get('term'))} {r.estimate:.3f} (SE {r.std_error:.3f})" for r in t3.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for i, (lab, g) in enumerate(t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)):
    for j, r in enumerate(g.itertuples()):
        ax.errorbar(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2, xerr=1.96 * r.std_error, fmt='o', color='#b22' if lab == "All" else '#222')
        ax.text(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2 + 0.08, lab, fontsize=7, ha='center')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(g))); ax.set_yticklabels(list(g.arm))
ax.axvline(0, color='#222', lw=0.5)
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("Effect on sharing vs True/neutral")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/E2_language.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white')
"}

import importlib.util, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)

d = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
pathlib.Path('results').mkdir(exist_ok=True); pathlib.Path('figures').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def fmt(r):
    return "; ".join(f"{a} {e:.3f} (SE {s:.3f})" for a, e, s in zip(r.arm, r.estimate, r.std_error))

h1 = reg.HYPOTHESES[0]
base = reg.reestimate(h1, d)
hp = dict(h1, outcome="plausibility")
pl = reg.reestimate(hp, d)
t1 = pd.concat([base.assign(outcome="share"), pl.assign(outcome="plausibility")])
t1.to_csv('results/E1_infotype_share_vs_plausibility.csv', index=False)
print("E1 Information type on sharing vs plausibility: " + fmt(base) + " | plausibility: " + fmt(pl))

rows = []
for lab, sub in [("All", d), ("English", d[d.survey_language == "English"]), ("Spanish", d[d.survey_language == "Spanish"])]:
    r = reg.reestimate(h1, sub); r["subset"] = lab; rows.append(r)
t2 = pd.concat(rows)
t2.to_csv('results/E2_infotype_by_language.csv', index=False)
print("E2 Information type effect on sharing by survey language: " + " | ".join(f"{l}: {fmt(g)}" for l, g in t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)))

d["older"] = (d.age > d.age.median()).astype(int)
t3 = reg.reestimate(h1, d, moderator="older")
t3.to_csv('results/E3_infotype_by_age.csv', index=False)
print("E3 Information type effect on sharing by age group: " + "; ".join(f"{row['arm']}/{row['level'] if 'level' in t3.columns else row['term']} {row['estimate']:.3f} (SE {row['std_error']:.3f})" for _, row in t3.iterrows()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for i, (lab, g) in enumerate(t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)):
    for j, r in enumerate(g.itertuples()):
        ax.errorbar(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2, xerr=1.96 * r.std_error, fmt='o', color='#b22' if lab == "All" else '#222')
        ax.text(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2 + 0.08, lab, fontsize=7, ha='center')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(g))); ax.set_yticklabels(list(g.arm))
ax.axvline(0, color='#222', lw=0.5)
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("Effect on sharing vs True/neutral")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/E2_language.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white')

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)

d = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
pathlib.Path('results').mkdir(exist_ok=True); pathlib.Path('figures').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def fmt(r):
    return "; ".join(f"{a} {e:.3f} (SE {s:.3f})" for a, e, s in zip(r.arm, r.estimate, r.std_error))

# E1 placebo-ish: effect on plausibility versus sharing (component outcome) -- plausibility outcome
h1 = reg.HYPOTHESES[0]
base = reg.reestimate(h1, d)
hp = dict(h1, outcome="plausibility")
pl = reg.reestimate(hp, d)
t1 = pd.concat([base.assign(outcome="share"), pl.assign(outcome="plausibility")])
t1.to_csv('results/E1_infotype_share_vs_plausibility.csv', index=False)
print("E1 Information type on sharing vs plausibility: " + fmt(base) + " | plausibility: " + fmt(pl))

# E2 robustness: drop respondents with age<25? use English-only and Spanish-only
rows = []
for lab, sub in [("All", d), ("English", d[d.survey_language == "English"]), ("Spanish", d[d.survey_language == "Spanish"])]:
    r = reg.reestimate(h1, sub); r["subset"] = lab; rows.append(r)
t2 = pd.concat(rows)
t2.to_csv('results/E2_infotype_by_language.csv', index=False)
print("E2 Information type effect on sharing by survey language: " + " | ".join(f"{l}: {fmt(g)}" for l, g in t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)))

t3 = reg.reestimate(h1, d, moderator="older")
t3.to_csv('results/E3_infotype_by_age.csv', index=False)
print("E3 Information type effect on sharing by age group: " + "; ".join(f"{r.arm}/{r.get('level', r.get('term'))} {r.estimate:.3f} (SE {r.std_error:.3f})" for r in t3.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for i, (lab, g) in enumerate(t2.groupby("subset", sort=False)):
    for j, r in enumerate(g.itertuples()):
        ax.errorbar(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2, xerr=1.96 * r.std_error, fmt='o', color='#b22' if lab == "All" else '#222')
        ax.text(r.estimate, j + i * 0.2 + 0.08, lab, fontsize=7, ha='center')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(g))); ax.set_yticklabels(list(g.arm))
ax.axvline(0, color='#222', lw=0.5)
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("Effect on sharing vs True/neutral")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/E2_language.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white')
"}

value.title: Information type on sharing vs plausibility
value.rationale: Comparing the effects on the plausibility judgment with those on sharing shows whether the sharing penalty tracks perceived credibility.
value.method: The effect of each headline type against true/neutral headlines was estimated for sharing and for the plausibility choice, using the same specification.
value.finding: Misinformation lowers sharing by 0.182 and plausibility by 0.186; fact-checks lower them by 0.133 and 0.124 (2 arms, 2 outcomes), so the two outcomes move almost identically.

value.title: Information type effect by survey language
value.rationale: The registered effects might differ between English and Spanish respondents, so the pooled estimate is checked in each language.
value.method: The registered information-type effect on sharing was re-estimated separately for English and Spanish survey respondents and compared with the full sample.
value.finding: Misinformation effect is -0.201 (SE 0.014) in English and -0.144 (SE 0.020) in Spanish; fact-check is -0.141 vs -0.119; both arms are negative in both languages, with a smaller penalty in Spanish.

value.title: Information type effect by respondent age
value.rationale: Age was not a planned moderator, and the PAP did not examine whether older respondents penalize false content differently.
value.method: The information-type effects on sharing were compared between respondents above and below the median age using interactions.
value.finding: Older respondents penalize misinformation more (interaction -0.078, SE 0.022), while the fact-check interaction is near zero (0.006, SE 0.023); 2 interactions tested.

You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished conjoint experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Describe the sample exactly as design.population.description says when it is given (e.g. 'US Latino adults', not 'US adults'); never widen it.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures. Write "p < 0.001" for any p-value below 0.001, never "p = 0.000".

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

Return ONLY JSON:
{"takeaways": [str, ...], "abstract": str, "design_notes": str, "results": {"H1": str, "H2": str, "S1": str, ...}, "exploratory": {"E1": str, ...}, "limitations": str}

- E3: Information type effect by respondent age — Older respondents penalize misinformation more (interaction -0.078, SE 0.022), while the fact-check interaction is near zero (0.006, SE 0.023); 2 interactions tested. [table results/E3_infotype_by_age.csv]

## Literature note
Prior work bearing on these hypotheses is thin and mostly general. Reviews of misinformation describe its spread and influence as a feature of the post-truth information environment (Lewandowsky et al., 2017). Reviews of conspiracy theories ask which factors are associated with conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019), which is relevant to the hypotheses about sharers who believe disputed claims. A cross-national study of COVID-19 misinformation examines predictors of belief in common false statements and links such belief to health behaviours (Roozenbeek et al., 2020). None of these works estimates how sharer attributes such as tie strength, trust, ideology, origin or knowledge affect willingness to share or the perceived plausibility of a post. The retrieved works do not directly disagree with one another or with the study's expectations, because none tests the same source-attribute effects. The nearest tension lies between accounts in which belief in misinformation drives behaviour (Roozenbeek et al., 2020) and the study's interest in sharing without believing (X4), in which sharing and plausibility judgments may come apart. The study's design, with randomized profile features and separate sharing and plausibility outcomes, can speak to that question. It cannot adjudicate the broader accounts of why people hold conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019).

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis with arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference level, so each
estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level instead of the
reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control group".
Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with that
level that were chosen) between two respondent groups; name the levels whose difference is distinguishable from zero.
design.features marks each feature randomized true/false. Only randomized features have causal AMCEs; for the others say
once, plainly, that they are measured attributes whose AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes, and
never call them randomized. The abstract and takeaways must cover the whole design, not only its largest effect: give the
randomized feature's effects one sentence, then the measured features that matter and the registered subgroup differences
that are distinguishable from zero. Large, expected main effects are not the news when the design was built to study the
other features.

## Hypotheses and subgroups tagged exploratory (ids like X1, XS1)
These were specified by the authors after seeing the data and are estimated by the same deterministic scripts as the
registered tests (not by model-written code). Write a results[<id>] note for each, as for the registered ones, and say once
that they are post hoc. They may appear in at most two takeaways, each introduced as exploratory, and must never qualify a
registered result in the abstract. The pipeline's own exploratory analyses (E1, E2, ...) remain unreviewed model code.

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) increased sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust raised sharing by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age, respondent ideology, respondent belief in disputed claims, trust in media, survey language.


The plan was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent chose between profiles, and the outcomes were being chosen to share and being judged more plausible. The headline type was randomized: true or neutral (the reference level), misinformation, or fact-check. The six sharer features describe the respondent's own real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. The sample is US Latino (Hispanic) adults from YouGov, surveyed in English or Spanish. All 12,000 raw rows entered analysis, with about 100 dropped from individual models for missing values. The reference group of true or neutral headlines has roughly 4,100 profiles. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Baseline sharing for true or neutral headlines was 60.3%. OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

## Exploratory analyses specified by the authors

*Not pre-registered. The authors specified these analyses after seeing the data; they are run by the same deterministic scripts as the registered tests and should be read as hypothesis-generating.*

<!-- fd:hyp id=X1 tag=exploratory outcome=share -->
### X1. A1. Trust in the sharer → sharing

*A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type.*  
*Exploratory, not pre-registered.*

Slope of Chosen to share on `trust_raw`: 0.014 (SE 0.004, p < 0.001, N = 11882). Significant at alpha = 0.05: yes.

This is a post hoc estimate. Each additional step of trust in the sharer (1-5) raised sharing by 1.4 points (SE 0.4, two-sided p < 0.001).

#### Details: model and coefficients (X1)

```
share ~ treat + close_num + origin_num + C(sharer_ideology) + knowledge_raw + conspiracy_raw

You are the checking agent in an automated review of a short research report on a conjoint experiment. You receive the report, its result tables, the registration status of its analysis plan, and the issues raised by one or more automated reviewers. You do four things and return ONLY JSON.

1. Pressure-test claims. Find every quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12, the most consequential first). For each, check it against the tables: the number, its sign, its interval, the outcome it is about, and whether the wording (e.g. "improved", "the only arm", "no effect") is justified. Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables).
2. Give every reviewer issue a disposition:
   - "address": a different or additional estimate on the same data would answer it (covariates, estimator, weights, sample, a robustness re-fit);
   - "editorial": only prose, labels, tables or missing detail need fixing;
   - "declined": answering it would change the pre-registered analysis (for example, a multiple-testing correction the plan does not specify, a different primary outcome). Say which part of the plan it conflicts with. Registered analyses are never changed to satisfy a reviewer;
   - "unresolved": the data cannot settle it (needs a new sample, a different design, a measure that was not collected), or reviewers disagree in a way the tables cannot resolve.
3. Corrections: at most 6, and ONLY to fix a reported number, sign, interval, significance statement or plan status (registered, deviation, exploratory). This is a Light Pass: no corrections about style, framing, interpretation, design or methods. Address the writing agent, never "the authors": no person revises this report.
4. Unresolved questions: return an empty list (a Light Pass only verifies estimates and plan statuses).

Return:

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-08 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->
![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: unreviewed](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #132,508](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: conjoint](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-08; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) increased sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust raised sharing by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age, respondent ideology, respondent belief in disputed claims, trust in media, survey language.


The plan was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent chose between profiles, and the outcomes were being chosen to share and being judged more plausible. The headline type was randomized: true or neutral (the reference level), misinformation, or fact-check. The six sharer features describe the respondent's own real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. The sample is US Latino (Hispanic) adults from YouGov, surveyed in English or Spanish. All 12,000 raw rows entered analysis, with about 100 dropped from individual models for missing values. The reference group of true or neutral headlines has roughly 4,100 profiles. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Baseline sharing for true or neutral headlines was 60.3%. Both are large, and this is the only randomized feature.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H2 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H2. Tie strength → sharing

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Profiles with a close tie were chosen 3.0 points more often than those with a distant tie (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], two-sided p = 0.003). This is a measured contrast rather than a randomized effect.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H3 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H3. Sharer origin → sharing

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Continental US origin differed from foreign origin by 0.2 points (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p = 0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero, though the interval rules out large effects.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

| Continental US | 0.002 | 0.008 | 0.8143 | [-0.014, 0.018] | 9400 | no |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H4 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H4. Sharer ideology → sharing

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], two-sided p = 0.034), a result near the threshold that should be read cautiously. A conservative sharer was within about 3 points of a liberal one in either direction (−0.7 points, 95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H4)

```

```

| Moderate sharer | -0.019 | 0.009 | 0.0337 | [-0.037, -0.001] | 6538 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.007 | 0.011 | 0.5470 | [-0.028, 0.015] | 2536 | no |

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished conjoint experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Describe the sample exactly as design.population.description says when it is given (e.g. 'US Latino adults', not 'US adults'); never widen it.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). ## Literature note
Prior work bearing on these hypotheses is thin and mostly general. Reviews of misinformation describe its spread and influence as a feature of the post-truth information environment (Lewandowsky et al., 2017). Reviews of conspiracy theories ask which factors are associated with conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019), which is relevant to the hypotheses about sharers who believe disputed claims. A cross-national study of COVID-19 misinformation examines predictors of belief in common false statements and links such belief to health behaviours (Roozenbeek et al., 2020). None of these works estimates how sharer attributes such as tie strength, trust, ideology, origin or knowledge affect willingness to share or the perceived plausibility of a post. The retrieved works do not directly disagree with one another or with the study's expectations, because none tests the same source-attribute effects. The nearest tension lies between accounts in which belief in misinformation drives behaviour (Roozenbeek et al., 2020) and the study's interest in sharing without believing (X4), in which sharing and plausibility judgments may come apart. The study's design, with randomized profile features and separate sharing and plausibility outcomes, can speak to that question. It cannot adjudicate the broader accounts of why people hold conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019).

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis with arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference level, so each
estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level instead of the
reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control group".
Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with that
level that were chosen) between two respondent groups; name the levels whose difference is distinguishable from zero.
design.features marks each feature randomized true/false. Only randomized features have causal AMCEs; for the others say
once, plainly, that they are measured attributes whose AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes, and
never call them randomized. The abstract and takeaways must cover the whole design, not only its largest effect: give the
randomized feature's effects one sentence, then the measured features that matter and the registered subgroup differences
that are distinguishable from zero. Large, expected main effects are not the news when the design was built to study the
other features.

## Revised report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-08 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->

Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age, respondent ideology, respondent belief in disputed claims, trust in media, survey language.


The plan was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent chose between profiles, and the outcomes were being chosen to share and being judged more plausible. The headline type was randomized: true or neutral (the reference level), misinformation, or fact-check. The six sharer features describe the respondent's own real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. The sample is US Latino (Hispanic) adults from YouGov, surveyed in English or Spanish. All 12,000 raw rows entered analysis, with about 100 dropped from individual models for missing values. The reference group of true or neutral headlines has 4,145 profiles. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Baseline sharing for true or neutral headlines was 60.3%. Both are large, and this is the only randomized feature.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H2 tag=registered outcome=share -->

*Pre-registered.*

Close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often than distant-tie profiles (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], two-sided p = 0.003). This is a measured contrast rather than a randomized effect.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

*Pre-registered.*

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], two-sided p = 0.034), a result near the threshold that should be read cautiously. A conservative sharer was −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]) relative to a liberal one.

<!-- fd:hyp id=H5 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H5. Trust in sharer → sharing

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on sharing: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

Neither mid nor high sharer knowledge was distinguishable from low knowledge. High knowledge was 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 3.9]), and mid knowledge was essentially level (95% CI [−2.0, 1.9]).

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on sharing: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age, respondent ideology, respondent belief in disputed claims, trust in media, survey language.


The plan was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent chose between profiles, and the outcomes were being chosen to share and being judged more plausible. The headline type was randomized: true or neutral (the reference level), misinformation, or fact-check. The six sharer features describe the respondent's own real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. The sample is US Latino (Hispanic) adults from YouGov, surveyed in English or Spanish. All 12,000 raw rows entered analysis, with about 100 dropped from individual models for missing values. The reference group of true or neutral headlines has 4,145 profiles. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

### H1. Information type → sharing

*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Baseline sharing for true or neutral headlines was 60.3%. Both are large, and this is the only randomized feature.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often than distant-tie profiles (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], two-sided p = 0.003). This is a measured contrast rather than a randomized effect.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Continental US origin differed from foreign origin by 0.2 points (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p = 0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero, though the interval rules out large effects.

<!-- fd:hyp id=H4 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H4. Sharer ideology → sharing

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], two-sided p = 0.034), a result near the threshold that should be read cautiously. A conservative sharer was −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]) relative to a liberal one.

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
Question: Do randomly assigned source trust and tie strength change willingness to share a false headline more than they change its perceived accuracy?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the design and measurement causes. Randomizing source cues turns the descriptive trust and tie contrasts into causal effects. Rating sharing and accuracy separately on 1–7 scales lets the two outcomes diverge.
Design sketch: Respondents see a single headline (true, false or fact-check) attributed to a fictional contact, with tie (close or distant) and trust (high or low) randomized, which gives a 3×2×2 factorial. Each respondent rates sharing intent and perceived accuracy on separate scales, and a subsample makes a real, incentivized share-or-not choice. Recruit US Latino YouGov adults, stratified by survey language.
Power target: about 1000 per arm to detect 0.05 at 80% power (Observed trust effect of 0.057 (H5) and MDE of 0.051 for Trust: high vs Trust: low. About 1,000 per cell gives an MDE near 0.05 on a 0/1 outcome; closer to 1,300 per cell is needed for the tie effect of 0.03 under clustering.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Is sharing misinformation driven by belief?): (a) Sharing tracks perceived plausibility, so susceptibility to misinformation is a belief problem and corrections should target accuracy. versus (b) Sharing and belief come apart depending on who the source is and on group or identity motives, so conspiracy-prone sharers or people may spread claims regardless of plausibility.. The source study says: Leans to position A on average, since the share and plausibility effects are nearly identical. Because both outcomes are forced choices and the sharer attributes are not randomized, it cannot test whether source attributes pull sharing away from plausibility. Respondents' belief in disputed claims raises misinformation sharing and plausibility alike (S3 and S8).

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

Key findings:
- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

Limitations: Only headline type was randomized, so effects of tie strength, trust, ideology, origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief are descriptive contrasts across respondents' real contacts, bundled with correlated attributes. Nearly eighty tests were run without multiplicity correction, so effects near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer contrast, deserve caution. Many subgroup contrasts rely on arms of a few hundred profiles, such as low-trust sharers. The post hoc exploratory tests were specified after seeing the data. The sample covers US Latino adults in a YouGov panel and may not generalize to other groups or platforms. Sharing was a forced choice between profiles, not real sharing behavior.

value.title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
value.rationale: The source study found misinformation lowered sharing by 18.2 points and plausibility by 18.6 points, so the two moved together. High trust (+5.7) and close tie (+3.0) were associated with more sharing, but sharer attributes were not randomized and both outcomes were forced choices. Randomizing source cues and rating sharing and accuracy separately lets the two outcomes diverge.
value.contribution: Tests causally whether source trust and tie strength shift sharing intent more than perceived accuracy of a false headline.
limitations: Fictional contact lacks real relationship history
Incentivized share is a subsample with a small stake
Single headline per respondent limits topic generalization
Stated trust and tie are vignette cues, not real relationships

design.title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
design.overview: US Latino adults see one headline (true, false or fact-check) attributed to a fictional contact whose tie (close or distant) and trust (high or low) are randomized, giving a 3x2x2 factorial. They rate sharing intent and perceived accuracy on separate 1-7 scales, then make a real share-or-not choice.
design.hypothesis: Source trust and tie strength raise sharing intent more than perceived accuracy, especially for the false headline.
design.primaryOutcome: Sharing intent (1-7) minus perceived accuracy (1-7, standardized), and each rating separately.
design.comparison: High vs low trust and close vs distant tie, on sharing versus accuracy, by headline type.
design.population: US Latino adults from YouGov, stratified by survey language (English or Spanish).
