messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'generalizability_conditional')
Type: generalizability_conditional (survey_experiment). Title: Replication across populations and languages
Question: Does the misinformation sharing penalty and the source-trust gradient hold in non-Latino and in Spanish- versus English-language samples?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.
Design sketch: Run the same conjoint with the same randomized headline type on matched YouGov samples of white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino respondents split by survey language. Keep the outcomes and registered moderators unchanged. Test whether the information-type effect varies by group and language.
Moderator or condition whose variation the design must cover: Population group and survey language
Power target: about 1500 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (The language gap is 0.057 (−0.201 vs −0.144), with SEs near 0.014–0.020. About 1,500 per group-by-arm cell gives an MDE near 0.04.); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

Key findings:
- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

Limitations: Only headline type was randomized, so effects of tie strength, trust, ideology, origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief are descriptive contrasts across respondents' real contacts, bundled with correlated attributes. Nearly eighty tests were run without multiplicity correction, so effects near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer contrast, deserve caution. Many subgroup contrasts rely on arms of a few hundred profiles, such as low-trust sharers. The post hoc exploratory tests were specified after seeing the data. The sample covers US Latino adults in a YouGov panel and may not generalize to other groups or platforms. Sharing was a forced choice between profiles, not real sharing behavior.

value.title: Replication across populations and languages
value.rationale: The source found a misinformation sharing penalty of −18.2 points and a fact-check penalty of −13.3 points, but only among US Latino adults, and the penalty looked smaller among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1). The language gap is confounded with sample, so this design runs the same headline-type randomization in white, Black, and Latino adults, with Latino adults split by survey language.
value.contribution: Tests whether the information-type penalty and the trust gradient generalize across racial/ethnic groups and survey languages.
limitations: Forced-choice sharing is not real sharing behavior.
Survey language is self-selected by Latino respondents, so the language contrast is not causal.
Sharer attributes remain measured, not randomized, so the trust gradient is descriptive.
Headline wording may translate imperfectly into Spanish.

design.title: Headline type effects on sharing across population groups and languages
design.overview: Adults from matched YouGov samples (white, Black, Latino-English, Latino-Spanish) name contacts, rate them, then complete four paired-headline trials with randomized headline type. Population group is a measured stratum, and headline type is randomized within it. The outcomes are the source study's.
design.hypothesis: The misinformation sharing penalty is negative in all groups, and it is smaller among Spanish-language Latino respondents than among English-language Latino respondents. High sharer trust is associated with more sharing in all groups.
design.primaryOutcome: Chosen to share (1 if the headline was chosen in 'Which post would you be more likely to share?')
design.comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, with the information-type by group and by language interaction tested. The fact-check vs true/neutral contrast is secondary.
design.population: US adults in YouGov samples: white, Black and Latino (English or Spanish survey language), matched on age, gender and education.

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'generalizability_conditional')
Type: generalizability_conditional (survey_experiment). Title: Replication across populations and languages
Question: Does the misinformation sharing penalty and the source-trust gradient hold in non-Latino and in Spanish- versus English-language samples?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.
Design sketch: Run the same conjoint with the same randomized headline type on matched YouGov samples of white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino respondents split by survey language. Keep the outcomes and registered moderators unchanged. Test whether the information-type effect varies by group and language.
Moderator or condition whose variation the design must cover: Population group and survey language
Power target: about 1500 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (The language gap is 0.057 (−0.201 vs −0.144), with SEs near 0.014–0.020. About 1,500 per group-by-arm cell gives an MDE near 0.04.); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

Key findings:
- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

Limitations: Only headline type was randomized, so effects of tie strength, trust, ideology, origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief are descriptive contrasts across respondents' real contacts, bundled with correlated attributes. Nearly eighty tests were run without multiplicity correction, so effects near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer contrast, deserve caution. Many subgroup contrasts rely on arms of a few hundred profiles, such as low-trust sharers. The post hoc exploratory tests were specified after seeing the data. The sample covers US Latino adults in a YouGov panel and may not generalize to other groups or platforms. Sharing was a forced choice between profiles, not real sharing behavior.

value.title: Replication across populations and languages
value.rationale: The source found a misinformation sharing penalty of −18.2 points and a fact-check penalty of −13.3 points, but only among US Latino adults. The penalty looked smaller among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), and that gap is confounded with sample. This design runs the same headline-type randomization in white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino adults split by survey language.
value.contribution: Tests whether the information-type penalty and the trust gradient generalize across racial/ethnic groups and survey languages.
limitations: Forced-choice sharing is not real sharing behavior.
Survey language is self-selected by Latino respondents, so the language contrast is not causal.
Sharer attributes remain measured, not randomized, so the trust gradient is descriptive.
Headline wording may translate imperfectly into Spanish.

design.title: Headline type effects on sharing across population groups and languages
design.overview: Adults from matched YouGov samples (white, Black, Latino-English, Latino-Spanish) rate a contact, then complete paired-headline trials with randomized headline type. Population group is a measured stratum, and headline type is randomized within it. The outcomes are the source study's.
design.hypothesis: The misinformation sharing penalty is negative in all groups, and it is smaller among Spanish-language Latino respondents than among English-language Latino respondents. High sharer trust is associated with more sharing in all groups.
design.primaryOutcome: Chosen to share (1 if the headline was chosen in 'Which post would you be more likely to share?')
design.comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, with the information-type by group and by language interaction tested. The fact-check vs true/neutral contrast is secondary.
design.population: US adults in YouGov samples: white, Black and Latino (English or Spanish survey language), matched on age, gender and education.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Belief-driven versus identity-driven sharing of misinformation
Question: Does sharing of a false claim follow its perceived plausibility, or does it vary with source ideology independently of plausibility?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the missing_moderator and design causes. Randomizing source ideology and measuring both outcomes lets sharing diverge from belief when sources are co-partisan, which the original could not test.
Design sketch: Show a false or true headline from a randomized source (co-ideological, opposed, or neutral) to respondents classified by their own ideology and belief in disputed claims. Measure accuracy judgements and sharing intent on separate scales, and test the interaction of source ideology with outcome in a within-subject design. If sharing follows belief, the source effect on both outcomes is the same; if identity drives sharing, the source effect on sharing exceeds its effect on accuracy.
Moderator or condition whose variation the design must cover: Respondent belief in disputed claims (tertiles)
Power target: about 1500 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (Moderator contrasts of about 0.055 (S3) with SEs near 0.017; the sharer ideology effect of 0.019 (H4) is smaller, so a cell of 1,500 targets an interaction MDE near 0.04.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Is sharing misinformation driven by belief?): (a) Sharing tracks perceived plausibility, so susceptibility to misinformation is a belief problem and corrections should target accuracy. versus (b) Sharing and belief come apart depending on who the source is and on group or identity motives, so conspiracy-prone sharers or people may spread claims regardless of plausibility.. The source study says: Leans to position A on average, since the share and plausibility effects are nearly identical. Because both outcomes are forced choices and the sharer attributes are not randomized, it cannot test whether source attributes pull sharing away from plausibility. Respondents' belief in disputed claims raises misinformation sharing and plausibility alike (S3 and S8).

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

Key findings:
- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

Limitations: Only headline type was randomized, so effects of tie strength, trust, ideology, origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief are descriptive contrasts across respondents' real contacts, bundled with correlated attributes. Nearly eighty tests were run without multiplicity correction, so effects near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer contrast, deserve caution. Many subgroup contrasts rely on arms of a few hundred profiles, such as low-trust sharers. The post hoc exploratory tests were specified after seeing the data. The sample covers US Latino adults in a YouGov panel and may not generalize to other groups or platforms. Sharing was a forced choice between profiles, not real sharing behavior.

You are the checking agent in an automated review of a short research report on a conjoint experiment. You receive the report, its result tables, the registration status of its analysis plan, and the issues raised by one or more automated reviewers. You do four things and return ONLY JSON.

1. Pressure-test claims. Find every quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12, the most consequential first). For each, check it against the tables: the number, its sign, its interval, the outcome it is about, and whether the wording (e.g. "improved", "the only arm", "no effect") is justified. Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables).
2. Give every reviewer issue a disposition:
   - "address": a different or additional estimate on the same data would answer it (covariates, estimator, weights, sample, a robustness re-fit);
   - "editorial": only prose, labels, tables or missing detail need fixing;
   - "declined": answering it would change the pre-registered analysis (for example, a multiple-testing correction the plan does not specify, a different primary outcome). Say which part of the plan it conflicts with. Registered analyses are never changed to satisfy a reviewer;
   - "unresolved": the data cannot settle it (needs a new sample, a different design, a measure that was not collected), or reviewers disagree in a way the tables cannot resolve.
3. Corrections: at most 6, and ONLY to fix a reported number, sign, interval, significance statement or plan status (registered, deviation, exploratory). This is a Light Pass: no corrections about style, framing, interpretation, design or methods. Address the writing agent, never "the authors": no person revises this report.
4. Unresolved questions: return an empty list (a Light Pass only verifies estimates and plan statuses).

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Among US Latino adults, a false headline was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than a true or neutral one (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less.
- Information type is the only randomized feature. Misinformation also lowered plausibility by 18.6 points (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4]), so sharing and plausibility moved together.
- Among measured sharer attributes, high trust was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing; the intervals rule out only large effects.
- Caveat: many tests were uncorrected, and the sharer attributes were not randomized, so their contrasts are descriptive; exploratory results are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age, respondent ideology, respondent belief in disputed claims, trust in media, survey language.


The plan was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent chose between profiles, and the outcomes were being chosen to share and being judged more plausible. The headline type was randomized: true or neutral (the reference level), misinformation, or fact-check. The six sharer features describe the respondent's own real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. The sample is US Latino (Hispanic) adults from YouGov, surveyed in English or Spanish. All 12,000 raw rows entered analysis, with about 100 dropped from individual models for missing values. The reference group of true or neutral headlines has 4,145 profiles. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Baseline sharing for true or neutral headlines was 60.3%. Both are large, and this is the only randomized feature.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

*Pre-registered.*

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)
